title: Suman 645 mil servicios y trámites a la población de Guanajuato con 156 mil visitas a hogares y 150 Ferias de Paz
content:
Suman 645 mil servicios y trámites a la población de Guanajuato con 156 mil visitas a hogares y 150 Ferias de Paz
La estrategia Atención a las Causas en Guanajuato sumó 645 mil servicios y trámites tras visitar 156 mil hogares y realizar más de 150 Ferias de Paz.
Con la estrategia de Atención a las Causas en Guanajuato, el Gobierno de México impulsó acciones en Celaya, Irapuato, León y Salamanca, donde se visitaron más de 156 mil hogares de colonias prioritarias y se realizaron más de 150 Ferias de Paz, lo cual permitió brindar 645 mil servicios y trámites a la población.
Durante la Conferencia del Pueblo de la Presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, la secretaria de Gobernación, Rosa Icela Rodríguez, también informó sobre los trabajos de la Mesa de Paz Estatal, encabezada por la gobernadora Libia Dennise García, así como de 10 Mesas Regionales, que sesionan de manera presencial todos los días.
Con el trabajo coordinado de los tres niveles de gobierno, precisó la secretaria, se llevaron a cabo 522 Jornadas por la Paz en los municipios donde se fomentaron actividades deportivas, culturales y artísticas.
La funcionaria federal precisó que, mediante la Secretaría de Desarrollo Agrario, Territorial y Urbano, se ejecutaron 21 obras dentro del “Programa Territorial para el Bienestar” con una inversión de más de 75 millones de pesos.
Además, como parte de la estrategia Jóvenes Transformando México, se construyen en el estado 14 nuevos bachilleratos Margarita Maza y un nuevo Bachillerato Tecnológico; se amplían dos CBTIS y un CETIS. También se edifican cuatro Centros Comunitarios “México Imparable”, en Celaya, Irapuato, León y Salamanca, que contarán con canchas de futbol 7, gimnasio de box, canchas de básquetbol y voleibol, áreas de ajedrez y servicios de salud mental para las y los jóvenes.
En tanto, la Comisión Nacional de Cultura Física y Deporte (Conade), en coordinación con la Comisión de Deporte local, impulsa el boxeo y baloncesto.
Invitamos a las y a los guanajuatenses a participar el domingo 27 de septiembre en la Clase Nacional de Baloncesto, “¡Ponte, Pila! ‘Bota y Encesta’”. Y a las niñas y niños, adolescentes y jóvenes les recordamos que pueden inscribirse de manera gratuita al programa Boxeando por la Paz”, subrayó.
La secretaria de Gobernación apuntó que hasta ahora se tienen 103 gimnasios, y más de 3 mil 600 alumnos aprenden este deporte.
Asimismo, en los cuatro Territorios de Paz, dijo, se realizó “Jóvenes Unen al Barrio” y se ha beneficiado a más de 4 mil personas con Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro.
Reconoció la participación ciudadana en las Jornadas Nacionales impulsadas por el Gobierno federal y el Instituto Mexicano de la Juventud (IMJUVE), con más de 5 mil actividades y un total de 261 mil participantes en tequios, torneos de futbol, murales, mosaicos y círculos de lectura.
Refirió que, en la entidad, con la colaboración de la Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional y la Iglesia Católica se promovió “Sí al Desarme, Sí a la Paz”. Del 1 de octubre de 2024 a la fecha, la población intercambió, de manera anónima y voluntaria, 639 armas de fuego por dinero en efectivo, en 12 municipios.

title: School feeding program inspected in Khatlon’s Yovon districtIn
content:
Representatives of the Russian Embassy in Tajikistan, the Ministry of Education and Science and the UN World Food Programme (WFP) have visited schools participating in the country’s state school feeding program in Yovon district, Khatlon province.
The delegation visited secondary schools No. 80, No. 45 and No. 35, where they reviewed the organization of school meals and the operation of cafeterias under the country’s State Program for School Feeding Development.
The officials also visited the district’s central bakery, which supplies fresh bread daily to elementary school students at participating schools.
The school feeding program is being implemented by the Tajik government in partnership with the WFP, with financial support from the Russian government. It currently covers around 460,000 elementary school students in nearly 2,000 schools across 60 cities and districtsof Tajikistan.
Students receive hot meals and bakery products on a daily basis.
WFP Representative, Country Director in Tajikistan, Mr. Siemon Hollema, said the organization had ensured an uninterrupted supply of food to schools from the start of the new academic year.
“WFP provided schools with the necessary food supplies in a timely manner. Deliveries will continue throughout the academic year, and preparations for school feeding in the next academic year are already underway,” Hollema said.
The program also provides support for renovating and equipping school cafeterias, bakeries and greenhouses, as well as technical assistance to improve the school nutrition system.
According to the WFP, the program contributes to improving children’s health and well-being and supports food security and the development of local capacity in Tajikistan.

title: Cameroon’s Banyo Plans 44 MW Solar Project Alongside Socadel Hybrid Program
content: A 44 MW solar photovoltaic project with battery storage is being developed in Banyo, in Cameroon’s Adamawa region. The new project is being promoted by the Foundation for Development of Ecology & Humankind, Fondecoh, in partnership with the Banyo municipal council and Supernova Energy, according to the Electricity Sector Regulatory Agency, Arsel. title: Students at the Indiana School for the Blind and Visually Impaired make coding more accessible
content:
Sign up for Chalkbeat Indiana’s free daily newsletter to keep up with Indianapolis Public Schools, Marion County’s township districts, and statewide education news.
Arabella Zink softly touches the keys of her laptop, leaning forward to listen to the voice coming from the computer speakers.
The seventh grader is building code, dragging and dropping elements on a screen to turn the educational technology known as micro:bit into a die. The small piece of educational technology, which connects to the computer in the shape of a chip, encourages students to learn to block code — a highly visual activity.
Arabella, however, does it without vision.
She’s one of seven students at the Indiana School for the Blind and Visually Impaired who helped develop a new accessibility feature for the micro:bit, expanding coding to blind and visually impaired students.
The accessibility initiative began last year, after the Micro:bit Educational Foundation reached out to the school’s media specialist, Shawn Humphrey. The foundation was seeking blind students who could read Braille to give input on screen reader compatibility and the accuracy of Braille instructions for visually impaired students, Humphrey said.
Arabella and her peers got to work, editing Braille materials and testing whether the screen reader could read what the computer was showing in a way they could understand within the Microsoft MakeCode program.
The project — developed with the foundation and the educational open source coding tools Microsoft MakeCode and Blockly — makes the micro:bit compatible with computer screen readers that tell students what is on their screen.
The micro:bit tool is used in 85 countries to bring coding to the classroom, with lessons that include how to program the tool to play games like rock, paper, scissors, or clap to turn on its lights. And now, with input from ISBVI students, coding is accessible not only to visually impaired students who use the Microsoft MakeCode platform, but all other coding programs built on Blockly’s software.
On a recent September afternoon, Arabella was learning how to make the micro:bit tool into a die that would light up with a number ranging from one to six when shaken. Students could identify which number it landed on by the number of beeps the micro:bit emitted after a shake.
Humphrey recalls seeing Arabella light up when she was told that she was one of the first students in the world to try a particular coding lesson using the accessible version of micro:bit.
“It’s one of the coolest things I’ve ever heard in education, having our students have that opportunity,” he said. “It has opened up coding for visually impaired students.”
Maddilyn Peters, a seventh grader with a penchant for horror stories who also helped develop the accessibility feature, has an interest in coding in order to make robots. Specifically, she said, she’d like to make animatronics like the ones in the horror film “Five Nights at Freddy’s” come to life.
“But not hostile,” she clarified. “I’m just going to make them not attack people.”
Amelia Pak-Harvey covers schools for Chalkbeat Indiana. Contact Amelia at apak-harvey@chalkbeat.org.

title: Where Can Russian Athletes Compete After the IOC’s Provisional Ban Lift?
content:
Russia’s return to international sports competition was already well underway long before the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally lifted its ban on the Russian and Belarusian Olympic Committees this July.
The shift began in September 2025, when the International Paralympic Committee voted against maintaining its ban on Russian and Belarusian athletes, paving the way for them to compete at the 2026 Milano-Cortina Paralympic Games, where Russian competitors won eight gold medals.
By December, the IOC recommended that international federations lift their bans on Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.
However, some individual governing bodies acted even earlier. The International Judo Federation became the first to restore full participation rights to senior Russian athletes in November of last year. World Taekwondo followed this January by approving the full return of both junior and senior athletes from Russia and Belarus.
Since then, eight additional Olympic sports federations have restored full participation rights to Russian athletes and teams, allowing the use of the Russian flag, national anthem and team uniforms.
Below is a list compiled by The Moscow Times detailing where and how Russian athletes can currently compete on the international stage:
Federations that allow full senior and youth participation
Archery: On August 14, World Archery reinstated Russian athletes, allowing them to compete under their national flag and bringing their status in line with Belarusian athletes, who were reinstated in May.
Aquatics: The World Aquatics Bureau lifted its ban on senior Russian and Belarusian athletes on April 13, 2026, two months after it lifted its ban on Junior athletes.
In its statement, World Aquatics President Husain Al Musallam said, “Over the last three years, World Aquatics and the AQIU have successfully helped ensure that conflict can be kept outside the sporting competition venues. We are determined to ensure that pools and open water remain places where athletes from all nations can come together in peaceful competition.”
Boxing: On July 30, World Boxing announced that it was restoring full participation rights to all Russian athletes.
"The Executive Committee accepted that Russian athletes would now take part in World Boxing competitions like boxers from any other national federation. However, World Boxing will strictly monitor the behaviour of Russian delegations during events as well as compliance with anti-doping protocols," the statement read.
World Boxing previously lifted its restrictions on Belarusian athletes on May 12.
Equestrian: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) will lift restrictions on Russian riders and officials starting Oct. 5 and once again allow international competitions to be held in Russia, the governing body has said.
FEI had already approved a return to competition for junior athletes from Russia and Belarus on May 19, 2026, but did not change its stance that senior athletes should compete with neutral status at that time.
Fencing: The International Fencing Federation (FIE) reinstated Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2, 2026.
“The decision reflects the FIE’s commitment to the fundamental principles of the Olympic Charter, including non-discrimination, equal treatment and the universality of sport, as well as the objectives and principles set out in the FIE Statutes,” FIE’s statement read.
On July 28, Russian fencer Pavel Graudyn won gold in the Men's individual sabre at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, marking Russia's first gold at a major championship since the International Fencing Federation lifted its restrictions.
Field Hockey: On Sept. 17, the Russian Field Hockey Federation announced that it had received a letter from the International Hockey Federation (FIH) lifting all restrictions against its athletes and national teams.
Gymnastics: The Executive Committee of World Gymnastics released a statement on May 18, 2026, that it had decided to lift all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts.
On July 28, 2026, European Gymnastics voted to bring itself in line with World Gymnastics in allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete with their national symbols.
Handball: On July 15, 2026, the International Handball Federation (IHF) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian teams and officials, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
“The IHF reiterates its longstanding commitment to the Ukraine Handball Federation and continues to stand in solidarity with Ukraine. It strongly condemns the ongoing war in Ukraine and its devastating consequences. It is the IHF’s sincere hope that the conflict will soon come to an end, paving the way for a return to peace, the restoration of normal sporting relations and the resumption of peaceful international cooperation,” the IHF statement said.
“At the same time, the IHF remains committed to safeguarding the values of sport, promoting dialogue within the international handball family, and ensuring that its decisions continue to reflect the recommendations of the IOC and the interests of the global handball community”
Judo: The International Judo Federation, calling sport the “last bridge for reconciliation and peace,” was the first to allow Russian and Belarusian senior athletes back, doing so on Nov. 27, 2025.
“Athletes have no responsibility for the decisions of governments or other national institutions, and it is our duty to protect the sport and our athletes,” the federation’s statement said.
“Sport must remain neutral, independent and free from political influence. Judo, rooted in the values of peace, unity and friendship, cannot allow itself to become a platform for geopolitical agendas. The decision to reinstate full national representation reflects the IJF’s confidence in its ethical safeguards, as well as in the strength and integrity of the sport,” it continued.
Modern Pentathlon: The International Union of Modern Pentathlon lifted its ban on Russian athletes on July 13, 2026, citing the IOC’s recommendation.
Taekwondo: The World Taekwondo Council allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes back into the fold on Jan. 31, 2026, at a meeting in the United Arab Emirates.
Triathlon: Mikhail Degtyarev, head of the Russian Olympic Committee and the Russian Minister of Sport, said on Aug. 21 that World Triathlon had granted Russian athletes full participation rights.
World Triathlon lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian junior athletes in April 2026, while senior athletes continue to compete as neutral athletes.
"This was made possible by the restoration of the Russian Olympic Committee's status. Earlier in April, World Triathlon already admitted Russian junior and para-athletes," Degtyarev said.
Volleyball: The International Volleyball Federation (FIVB) announced on July 8, 2026, that Russian teams and athletes would be restored to the World Ranking with the same World Ranking points they had at the time of the initial ban.
“The FIVB remains deeply concerned about the ongoing war in Ukraine and strongly condemns all forms of violence. We continue to hope for a peaceful resolution as soon as possible and remain committed to supporting the Ukrainian volleyball community through the FIVB Volleyball Empowerment programme,” FIVB added.
Weightlifting: The International Weightlifting Federation decided on June 26, 2026, to reinstate Russian and Belarusian athletes.
“The IWF remains committed to promoting fair competition, safeguarding the integrity of the sport and ensuring that athletes have the opportunity to compete in an environment that respects the principles of neutrality, inclusion and excellence,” the decision read.
Wrestling: United World Wrestling announced on May 15, 2026, that Russian and Belarusian wrestlers would be able to compete without restrictions starting with immediate effect.
Federations that allow full youth participation
Baseball/Softball: On Jan. 19, 2026, the World Baseball Softball Confederation (WBSC) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes. However, senior athletes remain banned.
Chess: The International Chess Federation (FIDE) lifted its ban on Russian and Belarusian youth chess players on Dec. 14, 2025. Senior athletes may compete under a neutral designation.
Curling: World Curling announced on Jan. 30, 2026, that, following the IOC’s recommendation, Russian and Belarusian junior athletes would be able to compete in international competition. Senior athletes remain unable to compete.
Sailing: The Russian Sailing Federation published a statement on June 9, 2026, announcing that the World Sailing Federation had approved a return to competition for Russian junior athletes.
Ski Mountaineering: The International Ski Mountaineering Federation (ISMF) reinstated Russian and Belarusian youth athletes.

title: السعودية تستهدف 72.3 مليون دولار للمنتجات المحلية
content:
تتجه «هيئة المحتوى المحلي والمشتريات الحكومية» إلى إضافة 81 منتجاً جديداً إلى القائمة الإلزامية للمنتجات الوطنية، بما تستفيد منها 77 مصنعاً في 9 قطاعات، وسط توقعات بزيادة الإنفاق الحكومي على المنتجات المحلية بنحو 271 مليون ريال (72.3 مليون دولار).
وتتوزع المنتجات الجديدة على قطاعات البناء والتشييد، والمواد الكيميائية والأسمدة، والقرطاسية والأدوات المكتبية، والنقل والخدمات اللوجستية، ومعدات ولوازم شخصية ومنزلية، وتقنية المعلومات، والأغذية والمنتجات الزراعية، والمستلزمات الطبية، والأدوية والمستحضرات الطبية.
ويتصدر قطاع المستلزمات الطبية قائمة المنتجات الجديدة بـ21 منتجاً، يليه قطاع الأدوية والمستحضرات الطبية بـ19 منتجاً، ثم قطاع البناء والتشييد بـ10 منتجات، والقرطاسية والأدوات المكتبية بـ8 منتجات، والنقل والخدمات اللوجستية بـ7 منتجات.
ومن حيث الإنفاق الحكومي المتوقع، يتصدر قطاع الأدوية والمستحضرات الطبية بـ75.9 مليون ريال (20.2 مليون دولار)، يليه قطاع تقنية المعلومات بـ63.4 مليون ريال (16.9 مليون دولار)، والنقل والخدمات اللوجستية بـ52.8 مليون ريال (14.1 مليون دولار)، والبناء والتشييد بـ24.5 مليون ريال (6.5 مليون دولار).
وتشمل القائمة كذلك 6 منتجات في قطاع المعدات، واللوازم الشخصية والمنزلية بإنفاق متوقع يبلغ 14 مليون ريال (3.7 مليون دولار)، و3 منتجات في قطاع الأغذية والمنتجات الزراعية بـ4.8 مليون ريال (1.3 مليون دولار)، و3 منتجات في قطاع المواد الكيميائية والأسمدة بـ3.5 مليون ريال (933 ألف دولار).
والجدير بالذكر أن الجهات المساهمة هي «وزارة الصناعة والثروة المعدنية»، «والهيئة السعودية للمواصفات والمقاييس والجودة»، «وهيئة كفاءة الإنفاق والمشروعات الحكومية (إكسبرو)»، «واتحاد الغرف السعودية».

title: After the Ballot, the Building Begins: From a Record of Delivery to Five More Years of Turning Public Trust Into Progress
content:
After the Ballot, the Building Begins: From a Record of Delivery to Five More Years of Turning Public Trust Into Progress
Addis Ababa, September 22, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s seventh general election has closed one political cycle and opened another: from campaigning and voting to governing, delivering and building.
With the Prosperity Party securing 438 of the 501 seats in the House of Peoples’ Representatives, the electoral outcome has cleared the way for the formation of the next federal government and a new five-year governing period.
But the significance of the post-election moment extends beyond the formation of a new cabinet.
The more consequential phase begins after the ballot box—when electoral commitments must enter the machinery of government, development plans must become implemented programmes, and the confidence expressed through voting must increasingly be matched by tangible outcomes.
That makes the coming five years both a continuation and a new test. The government does not begin this cycle from a blank page. It carries forward a record accumulated over the previous eight years, alongside unfinished tasks and new commitments that will define the next stage of Ethiopia’s national project.
The record itself spans an unusually broad development landscape.
Since 2018, Ethiopia has pursued reforms intended to move the economy toward a more diversified and market-oriented model, while simultaneously attempting to raise agricultural productivity, expand manufacturing, reform financial and telecommunications sectors, attract investment and strengthen domestic productive capacity.
In its April 2026 assessment, the Office of the Prime Minister reported that agricultural output had risen from 41.7 million tons to around 150 million tons over seven years, while Ethiopia had reached wheat self-sufficiency and emerged as Africa’s largest wheat producer by 2024/25.
The same assessment reported the expansion of cluster farming to 9.5 million farmers across 12.8 million hectares, accompanied by reported gains in productivity and incomes.
The transformation has also been visible in sectors far removed from the traditional image of development. Digital public infrastructure has become a central component of the state’s modernization agenda.
Fayda, digital payments, national data exchange, cybersecurity infrastructure, digital skills and integrated government services are being developed as interconnected elements of Digital Ethiopia 2030. MESOB, in particular, is designed to provide integrated, user-centred government services through digital portals, applications and service centres.
The environmental agenda has likewise evolved into a major national development undertaking. The Green Legacy initiative has expanded from a tree-planting campaign into a broader programme associated with landscape restoration, watershed rehabilitation, climate resilience and green development.
These initiatives, alongside major infrastructure and energy investments, illustrate the breadth of the development agenda that the incoming administration will inherit.
The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam stands among the most consequential examples of that long-term national investment.
Built through domestic financing and sustained public mobilisation, the project has moved from a national construction undertaking into a major component of Ethiopia’s energy strategy and its wider regional water and power landscape.
The same pattern can be seen in agriculture, where irrigation and productivity programmes are changing the relationship between farming and climatic uncertainty.
Irrigated wheat production, for example, has been pursued not merely as an agricultural intervention but as part of a broader effort to strengthen food security, reduce import dependence, conserve foreign exchange and create a more resilient production system.
These developments provide the backdrop against which the next five-year mandate should be understood.
The question is no longer simply whether Ethiopia can launch large national programmes.
It is whether the country can consolidate what has been built, deepen institutional capacity, improve implementation, broaden the benefits of growth and convert major projects into durable improvements in citizens’ lives.
The post-election period therefore places delivery at the centre of governance.
The Prosperity Party’s election manifesto, launched ahead of the June 1 vote under the theme “Ethiopia Towards an Exemplary Nation!”, presented productivity, prosperity and collective national advancement as central elements of its programme.
Following the announcement of the final results, the party reaffirmed commitments to democratic governance, development and national unity.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has likewise described the renewed public mandate as carrying a heightened responsibility for governance, institutional strengthening and continued development.
In remarks following the election, he linked the government’s next phase to improving governance, strengthening public institutions, combating corruption, enhancing transparency and accountability, and translating electoral confidence into concrete improvements in economic development and national unity.
That transition from mandate to implementation is where the meaning of the next five years will increasingly be measured.
A government entering a second consecutive five-year cycle faces a different political and administrative task from one beginning its first. Its accumulated record becomes part of the public benchmark.
Projects already initiated must reach their intended scale and impact; reforms must mature into institutions; successful experiments must be replicated; and new promises must be judged not only by their ambition but by their execution.
For Ethiopia, that means moving from individual achievements toward systems capable of sustaining them.
The digital transformation must increasingly translate connectivity, identity, artificial intelligence and digital public infrastructure into productivity and accessible services. Agricultural advances must develop into more diversified, climate-resilient and commercially connected food systems.
Energy investments must support industrialization and broader economic productivity. Urban development must produce more liveable and economically productive cities. Manufacturing must deepen domestic value chains. Environmental programmes must continue building ecological resilience. And institutional reforms must make delivery more predictable, accountable and responsive.
The scale of the challenge is matched by the scale of the opportunity.
The seventh election was held on June 1, with more than 54 million citizens registered to vote. NEBE’s post-election process included the verification and review of results and the handling of complaints before the final outcome was announced on June 21.
Regional and international actors, including IGAD, subsequently recognized the conduct of the electoral process and emphasized the importance of continued democratic governance, constitutional order and institutional development.
That process now gives way to a different kind of democratic accountability: the accountability of governing.
The ballot provides a constitutional mechanism through which citizens confer political authority. Government performance, in turn, provides one of the principal ways that authority is translated into public experience. Roads completed, power generated, crops harvested, services delivered, technologies deployed, jobs created, institutions strengthened and reforms implemented are ultimately where the abstract language of a mandate acquires practical meaning.
This is why the next five years should not be viewed merely as another administrative interval.
They represent the next phase in a longer national trajectory—one in which Ethiopia is attempting to consolidate economic reform, technological modernization, infrastructure expansion, agricultural transformation, environmental restoration and institutional development within a single national development project.
The measure of the new period will therefore lie not only in the promises placed before the public, but in the distance between those promises and their realization.
The country enters that period with a substantial body of work already under construction and an even larger agenda ahead. The election has supplied the political transition.
The next five years will determine how effectively that mandate is converted into institutions, infrastructure, productivity, opportunity and measurable improvements in national life.
The ballot has spoken. The next chapter is written through delivery.

title: If India Is Spending Crores on Its Cities, Nature Must Count as Infrastructure
content:
Indian cities have a familiar response to flooding, heat and water stress—build more. Bigger drains, higher embankments, longer pipelines and more concrete infrastructure are often treated as the default answer.
But India is now at a moment when that instinct must be reconsidered.
The Union government’s Rs 1 lakh crore Urban Challenge Fund, operationalised in April 2026, is intended to catalyse about Rs 4 lakh crore of urban investment over five years.
Central assistance can cover 25 percent of project cost, while at least 50 percent is expected from market sources. Its ambition is to create resilient, productive, inclusive and climate-responsive cities.
That is a major opportunity. It also raises a basic question: when cities compete for finance, what will count as infrastructure?
A flyover has a project cost. A sewage plant has a contract. A restored wetland, urban lake, floodplain or green corridor may reduce flooding, cool neighbourhoods and recharge groundwater, but those benefits are harder to place on a municipal balance sheet.
If “bankability” is interpreted too narrowly, India could end up financing what is easiest to monetise rather than what makes cities most resilient.
Nature Already Performs Urban Services
The case is especially clear in urban flooding. In July, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs acknowledged that intense rainfall is only part of the problem. Unplanned growth, encroachment of natural water bodies and inadequate drainage also compound flooding. The ministry’s own river-centric planning guidance recognises nature-based solutions.
Yet wetlands, lakes, floodplains and permeable open spaces are still too often treated as environmental amenities rather than working urban assets.
A wetland can temporarily store stormwater. A floodplain gives a river room to expand. Vegetated areas slow runoff and help water infiltrate the soil. Trees and green spaces can reduce local heat exposure. These services do not eliminate the need for drains, pumps or engineered flood protection. But they can reduce the burden placed on them.
The choice, therefore, is not nature versus engineering. The smarter model is blue-green-grey infrastructure, where ecological and engineered systems are planned together.
This matters because India’s new urban finance architecture is explicitly market-linked. Nature-based projects often struggle not because they lack public value, but because avoided flood losses, lower heat exposure and groundwater recharge do not produce simple cash flows.
A 2026 guidebook from the India Forum for Nature-based Solutions also highlighted the need to strengthen financing models if urban NbS are to scale.
Make Nature Investible, Without Turning it into a Slogan
The Urban Challenge Fund can help change this, but only if natural infrastructure is deliberately built into project appraisal.
- First, eligible projects should be able to include restoration of wetlands, lakes, river buffers, watersheds and urban green systems as core infrastructure components, not decorative add-ons.
- Second, appraisal should recognise avoided costs and public benefits.
If restoring a wetland reduces peak runoff and lowers the need for additional drainage, that value should be visible in the economic assessment.
- Third, cities seeking finance for major flood-management or heat-resilience projects should show that nature-based and hybrid alternatives were assessed alongside conventional engineering options.
This does not mean forcing a green solution where it will not work. It means asking the question before automatically reaching for concrete.
- Fourth, nature-based projects must be measured as rigorously as conventional infrastructure.
Funding should be tied to outcomes such as water retained, flood exposure reduced, canopy maintained, or temperature moderated. Planting trees or fencing a lake cannot, by itself, be treated as success.
Calling something “nature-based” does not make it effective. Poorly designed restoration can fail just as poorly designed grey infrastructure can.
The Money Is Arriving. The Rules Should Reward Resilience
The Urban Challenge Fund matters not only because of its size, but because it can influence what municipalities and investors begin to consider financeable.
If urban resilience is judged mainly through assets that generate direct revenue, natural systems will remain underfunded even when they provide essential public services. But if city finance begins recognising reduced risk, avoided costs and measurable resilience outcomes, wetlands, floodplains and urban forests can move from the margins of environmental planning into the centre of infrastructure strategy.
India does not need to choose between concrete and nature. It needs to stop financing cities as though only one of them counts.
If Rs 1 lakh crore of public support is going to reshape urban India, it should help build cities that work with their natural systems, not cities that pay to replace them after they are gone.
(The author is a Senior Associate Fellow, Land Resources Division, The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI). This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)

title: After years of complaints, Missouri tenants win nearly $4M, debt relief, and repairs
content:
A yearslong fight over neglected housing conditions at a Kansas City apartment complex has ended with a major court-ordered settlement, underscoring how renters often have to organize for years just to secure basic repairs and recover what they have lost.
Here's what to know
The case centers on Stonegate Meadows in Kansas City, Missouri, where tenants said ownership left major problems unresolved, including rodents, roaches, and plumbing trouble, and the class-action litigation has now produced almost $4 million in settlements.
According to KCTV, the Jackson County court order requires repairs at the property and sends $2 million to eligible tenants, bringing the total class-action settlements to nearly $4 million. A release from the Heartland Center for Jobs and Freedom does not project the total number of eligible tenants, but it notes that there are 366 units and "hundreds of families" who can benefit from the order.
@kctv5 After years of legal battles, tenants at a Kansas City apartment complex are finally getting a settlement. #stonegate #legalbattle ♬ original sound - KCTV5
Even with the settlement, some tenants said the complex still faces unresolved issues.
"Does this feel like a win or is it like a start? I won't really say it feels like a win because it's still problems going on," resident Michele Williams said. "People still having the issues that we was having when we stayed on the property."
Anyone who lived at Stonegate between December 1, 2019, and May 5, 2026, is included in the settlement. People seeking more information can call 1-866-742-4955 or visit bit.ly/StonegateSettlement.
More background
Pest infestations, plumbing failures, and deferred maintenance can create health risks, disrupt work and school routines, and force families to spend money to replace damaged belongings or cover temporary fixes.
The court's response in this case includes both repair orders and financial compensation.
Organizers urged people facing similar conditions to keep documenting issues, keep reporting them, and keep speaking up until they find justice.
For renters hoping to change restrictive property rules before conditions worsen, collective action can matter there too.
"Like we can do the things that we need to do, pay back the things we need to pay back, collect what we lost," Williams said. "That's the main thing, collect what we lost."
Where can I learn more?
Disputes like this one can drag on for years over repairs, fees, and who is responsible for fixing the problem.
• In Phoenix, an apartment resident blasted wasteful irrigation practices while management ignored courtyard problems.
• A tenant in a rental community faced HOA lawn maintenance demands months before moving out.
• A frustrated renter refused to send them pictures after an HOA demanded proof of upkeep.
• Families in one neighborhood pushed for an investigation into HOA amenity charges they never used.
• A tenant watched an upstairs neighbor's foul habit ruin the backyard view below.

title: Ukraine brings back 15 people from Russian occupation, including 96-year-old woman
content:
Ukraine brings back 15 people from Russian occupation, including 96-year-old woman
Another 15 Ukrainians have been brought back from territories temporarily occupied by Russia, including a 96-year-old woman from Kherson Oblast, the oldest of those rescued.
Source: Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets on Facebook
Details: A 74-year-old man managed to leave Kakhovka. He had lived under occupation for years because he feared that leaving could harm his son, who was being held captive by Russia. When his son was released in 2025, the father also decided to leave for territory controlled by Ukraine.
However, other problems had emerged by then: his health had deteriorated over the years. He had suffered a severe stroke, which left him partially paralysed, and developed inflammation of the submandibular gland.
He is now being treated by doctors and experts are helping him reinstate his documents, as Ukrainians returning from the occupation often have expired or lost IDs. He will meet his relatives for the first time in years.
A 96-year-old woman left the occupied village of Zaliznyi Port in Kherson Oblast together with her daughter and son-in-law. The family had been living amid attacks, power outages and food shortages.
The elderly woman required constant assistance, while her son-in-law was using an Ilizarov apparatus on his lower limb. Because of this, they could not leave the occupied territory on their own.
The family is now safe, and the grandmother will have the opportunity to see her grandson.
"Everyone who returns has their own reason for waiting for this day. Some will finally be able to embrace their loved ones after years of occupation. Some will be able to see doctors. And some simply want to be safe. For everyone, it means one thing: no longer living in fear," Lubinets added.
Background: A group of 32 Ukrainian children and teenagers was previously brought back from the occupation. Among them was a six-year-old boy who suffered severe psychological trauma after witnessing a drone strike near a children's playground.

title: From Moruca to Sandhurst: Fianna Tading Blazes a New Trail
content:
At just 18, Officer Cadet Fianna Maria Tading has turned a determination to build a better future for herself and her sisters into a historic milestone for the Guyana Defence Force (GDF).
Five months into the GDF’s Standard Officer Course Number 58 (SOC #58), Tading was selected for training at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in the United Kingdom, becoming the first woman in the history of the GDF to be selected for training at the prestigious military academy.
The distinction is important: Tading has not yet begun training at Sandhurst. She remains an officer cadet undergoing SOC #58, and her selection represents an opportunity for further professional military training once she moves on to the Sandhurst programme. Her current responsibility is to continue her officer-cadet training while preparing for that next stage.
Her achievement comes as the GDF approaches its 61st anniversary. The Force came into existence on November 1, 1965, when training began under a team of British instructors, less than seven months before Guyana gained independence.
The GDF was established under the government of Premier Forbes Burnham, whose People’s National Congress (PNC) was then in coalition with the United Force (UF). Guyana was still British Guiana when the Force was formed. It was built from personnel drawn from the British Guiana Volunteer Force, Special Service Unit, British Guiana Police Force and civilian volunteers.
Following independence on May 26, 1966, the GDF became part of the institutional framework of the new nation. Over the decades, it developed its own officer-training system while maintaining links with overseas military institutions. The Colonel Ulric Pilgrim Officer Cadet School was established in 1981, while GDF personnel have continued to pursue professional military training abroad, including at Sandhurst.
Against that history, Tading’s selection represents another milestone in the evolution of the Force and the advancement of women within its ranks.
From Moruca to the Officer Corps
Tading’s journey began in Moruca, Region One (Barima-Waini), and has been shaped by determination, family support and the encouragement of a teacher who recognised her potential.
Now residing at Strathspey on the East Coast Demerara, she completed her secondary education at Bladen Hall Multilateral School. Her interest in military service grew after a teacher encouraged her to apply for the GDF’s Standard Officer Course.
The challenge itself became part of the attraction.
“Life was a bit tough for us growing up, and I always wanted a better future for myself and my sisters. When I learnt how challenging the officer course was, I decided that it was a challenge I wanted to take on,” she said.
After successfully completing the rigorous initial assessments for prospective officer cadets, Tading began training on SOC #58. Five months into the course, her performance earned her selection for further training at Sandhurst.
The opportunity came unexpectedly, but she sees it as an important step in her development as a military officer.
“The opportunity was unexpected, but I am extremely grateful. I see it as an important step towards becoming a military officer. I intend to give my best, learn as much as I can and return better prepared to serve the GDF and share what I have learnt,” she said.
A Historic Chapter for Women
Women have been part of the GDF almost from its earliest years. The Force recruited its first four female officers in January 1967, shortly after independence. They included Joan Granger, Brenda Aaron, Hyacinth King and Clarissa Hookumchand. By 1969, women were being exposed to combat training as the Force expanded the roles available to them.
Tading’s Sandhurst selection adds another milestone to that history.
The significance extends beyond being the first woman from the GDF selected for training at Sandhurst. The Royal Military Academy is one of the United Kingdom’s principal institutions for military officer training, and the GDF identifies Sandhurst among the overseas institutions where its personnel receive professional military training.
Tading’s selection places her within a wider tradition of Guyanese military personnel pursuing advanced training abroad and returning with knowledge and experience to contribute to the development of the Force.
The People Behind the Achievement
Tading does not present the achievement as hers alone.
She credits her sisters with helping her navigate the demands of her journey, particularly her older sister, Jarilene Henry, whom she describes as her “rock and constant support.”
That support has accompanied her from her formative years through the demanding environment of officer-cadet training and now toward an opportunity that could take her to the United Kingdom.
Her story also underscores the influence that a single teacher can have on a young person’s future. Encouragement to apply for an officer course became the first step in a journey that has taken Tading from Moruca to a historic selection for one of the world’s best-known military academies.
A Message to Young Guyanese
As she continues SOC #58 and prepares for her prospective Sandhurst training, Tading hopes her achievement will encourage other young Guyanese, particularly young women, to consider careers in the GDF.
“I am grateful to the GDF for affording me this opportunity, and I am happy that I made the decision to join. I would encourage young people who are willing to work hard, challenge themselves and serve Guyana to consider a career in the GDF,” she said.
Her journey began with a decision to embrace a demanding challenge because she believed it could help create a better future.
Five months into SOC #58, that decision has already made GDF history.
The Sandhurst chapter has yet to begin. Tading’s immediate task remains her current officer-cadet training. The next stage, if completed as planned, will take her into further professional military development at Sandhurst before she returns to continue her career and service in the GDF.
From a young woman encouraged by a teacher to take a chance, to the first female GDF officer cadet selected for Sandhurst training, Tading’s story illustrates how determination, opportunity and support can open doors far beyond the circumstances in which a journey begins.
Her achievement is personal, but it also marks another chapter in the evolving story of women in Guyana’s military—and offers young Guyanese another example of where discipline, perseverance and a willingness to accept a challenge can lead.

title: Bổ sung chế độ bảo vệ người thân của thẩm phán
content:
Bổ sung chế độ bảo vệ người thân của thẩm phán
Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội thông qua nguyên tắc nghị quyết về chế độ bảo vệ thẩm phán với nhiều nội dung quan trọng liên quan vợ chồng và người thân.
Sáng 24/9, Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội xem xét, thông qua dự thảo Nghị quyết quy định về chế độ bảo vệ thẩm phán.
Nghị quyết áp dụng các quy trình, thủ tục bảo vệ thẩm phán khi thi hành công vụ hoặc trong trường hợp cần thiết. Thân nhân của thẩm phán (gồm vợ hoặc chồng, cha mẹ đẻ, cha mẹ vợ hoặc chồng, cha mẹ nuôi, con đẻ và con nuôi) được bảo vệ khi tính mạng, sức khỏe, tài sản, quyền và lợi ích hợp pháp khác bị xâm phạm hoặc đe dọa xâm phạm liên quan công việc của thẩm phán.
Người thân có thể được đưa đến nơi an toàn
Cơ quan có thẩm quyền có thể yêu cầu người vi phạm chấm dứt hành vi xâm phạm; đưa thẩm phán hoặc thân nhân đến nơi an toàn; áp dụng biện pháp ngăn chặn, không cho đối tượng liên quan tiếp cận; giữ bí mật hoặc thay đổi thông tin, dữ liệu cá nhân, nơi ở, nơi làm việc. Trong trường hợp cần thiết, lực lượng, phương tiện và công cụ có thể được bố trí để trực tiếp bảo vệ an toàn cho thẩm phán và thân nhân.
UBND các cấp được giao tiếp nhận thông tin, chủ động nắm bắt tình hình nơi thẩm phán và thân nhân cư trú; chỉ đạo công an cấp xã và các đơn vị liên quan thực hiện biện pháp phòng ngừa, ngăn chặn khi phát sinh tình huống.
Nếu tính mạng, sức khỏe của thẩm phán hoặc thân nhân bị đe dọa do công việc của thẩm phán, Chánh án có thể đề nghị cơ quan công an, đơn vị quân đội có thẩm quyền áp dụng biện pháp bảo vệ.
Chánh án TAND Tối cao Nguyễn Văn Quảng cho biết nguy cơ thẩm phán bị đe dọa, tác động, trả thù hoặc xâm hại khi thi hành công vụ là vấn đề hiện hữu. Nhiều vụ án tham nhũng, kinh tế, chức vụ, tranh chấp đất đai, khiếu kiện hành chính kéo dài hoặc có nhiều người tham gia tố tụng dễ phát sinh mâu thuẫn. Thẩm phán có thể bị tác động, can thiệp trái pháp luật, đe dọa, xúc phạm danh dự, uy tín, thậm chí xâm phạm sức khỏe, tính mạng trong quá trình thực hiện nhiệm vụ.
Các hành vi xâm phạm xảy ra dưới nhiều hình thức, từ xúc phạm, đe dọa, gây áp lực, cản trở hoạt động xét xử đến hành hung, tấn công trực tiếp. Những vụ việc này không chỉ xảy ra tại phòng xử án mà còn trong quá trình xem xét, thẩm định tại chỗ, hòa giải hoặc làm việc với đương sự.
Vì vậy, việc ban hành Nghị quyết về chế độ bảo vệ thẩm phán là cần thiết nhằm phòng ngừa, ngăn chặn hành vi xâm phạm, bảo đảm an toàn cho thẩm phán và bảo vệ tính độc lập của hoạt động xét xử.

title: Advancing disaster and climate resilience through people-centred approaches in rural Zimbabwe: an Afrocentric perspective
content: IntroductionThis study aimed to explore how disaster and climate resilience can be achieved through people-centred approaches in rural Zimbabwe using the Afrocentric framework. This was against the backdrop of the application of resilience in policy, practice, and academic discourses still being shaped by technocratic, Eurocentric, and top-down models that marginalise local realities, knowledge, and worldviews.MethodsA qualitative research approach was adopted, in which data were collected through talking circles and semi-structured interviews from purposively selected participants in the Chimanimani district. These include traditional leaders, community members, government officials and development agencies.ResultsThe Reflexive Thematic Content Analysis was adopted to establish meaning in the data. The findings highlight a disconnect between rhetoric and genuine participation, with most interventions remaining externally defined and elite-driven. Through the Afrocentric analytical tool, the study affirms that genuine people-centred approaches reposition indigenous knowledge systems as legitimate and independent epistemologies instead of being auxiliary to scientific knowledge. It further demonstrates that alternative expressions of resilience, such as Kutsungirira (perseverance), represent unique cultural, spiritual and ontological frameworks that represent the plurality of resilience. The study further surfaced that people-centred approaches reinforce inclusivity, social cohesion, and collective action that address vulnerabilities and marginalisations.DiscussionThese findings are a step forward in decolonising resilience by advancing Afrocentricity as an analytical epistemological tool for reimagining resilience beyond neoliberal and top-down framings and actions in natural hazards, climate change, and disaster settings.

title: Julie Gobert créée un groupe dédié aux parents solos pour briser la solitude et trouver de l’entraide à Mons : “Ce n’est pas toujours facile à vivre”
content:
Julie Gobert créée un groupe dédié aux parents solos pour briser la solitude et trouver de l'entraide à Mons : "Ce n'est pas toujours facile à vivre"
Garder les enfants, retrouver un logement, profiter d'un événement, recréer du lien, ce sont les objectifs affichés du groupe "Parents solo Mons"
- Publié le 19-09-2026 à 16h01
Être parent solo, c'est parfois devoir tout gérer seul : les enfants, les imprévus, les finances, mais aussi les moments où l'on aurait simplement besoin de souffler. Dans la Cité du Doudou, Julie Gobert a décidé de créer un espace pour permettre à ces parents de se retrouver et de s'entraider. Baptisé "Parents Solo Mons", son groupe Facebook compte déjà 145 membres, quelques semaines seulement après son lancement.
Montoise et maman solo de deux garçons de 6 et 13 ans, Julie Gobert connaissait déjà le groupe "Parents Solo Belgique". "C'est un groupe hypersolidaire, il y a beaucoup de publications chaque jour, que ce soit sur la garde des enfants, les pensions alimentaires, le mal-être… Il y a énormément de témoignages et de solidarité", souligne-t-elle. "C'est aussi une façon de partager des événements qui pourraient intéresser les membres."
Mais le groupe national couvre toute la Belgique. "Il faut donc parfois parcourir de nombreux kilomètres pour participer à une activité." D'où l'idée de créer une déclinaison montoise, davantage ancrée localement. "Le but, c'est de rassembler, de faire de nouvelles rencontres et de pouvoir aussi se rencontrer dans la réalité sans avoir à traverser la Belgique. La proximité, dans ce genre de situation, cela peut aussi être une force et une aide précieuse."
S'entraider aussi dans les moments difficiles
Depuis la création du groupe, les demandes d'adhésion arrivent quotidiennement. Sorties, bons plans, garde d'enfants, repassage ou encore événements, chacun peut partager ses besoins ou ses propositions. Pour Julie Gobert, cette entraide peut également prendre une dimension plus concrète lorsque la situation devient compliquée. Elle pense notamment aux parents qui se séparent et doivent rapidement trouver un logement.
"Quand on devient solo, c'est très difficile. Moi-même, au début, je partageais encore la maison familiale et j'avais besoin de trouver un autre logement, ne serait-ce que temporairement, pour pouvoir souffler, avoir ma propre chambre. Mais trouver rapidement, et dans un contexte financier qui est lui aussi changeant n'est pas simple." Elle imagine dès lors des formes d'entraide comme de petites colocations entre parents solos. "Ce serait une situation transitoire, le temps de se retourner, de vendre la maison ou de retrouver un logement après la séparation."
Elle-même se dit prête à aller dans ce sens : "J'ai une chambre que je peux mettre à disposition d'un parent solo qui se retrouverait dans une situation compliquée." Au-delà des difficultés matérielles, c'est surtout le lien social que Julie Gobert souhaite recréer. "Nous vivons dans une société de surcommunication et pourtant, nous n'avons jamais été aussi seuls, surtout lorsque notre situation amoureuse chance. Personnellement, si je n'avais pas eu mes amis pour me sortir et me faire bouger, je ne sais pas où j'en serais."
À 42 ans, l'éducatrice spécialisée est par ailleurs actuellement à la recherche d'un nouveau défi professionnel, notamment dans les domaines de l'assistance commerciale ou administrative. Une nouvelle étape dans un parcours où l'envie de créer du lien et d'aider les autres reste bien présente. Le groupe "Parents Solo Mons" est ouvert aux parents solos de la région. L'objectif de Julie Gobert est désormais de continuer à le faire grandir, mais surtout de transformer les échanges virtuels en véritables rencontres.

title: Skupština Istarske županije traži ukidanje odluke o spaljivanju otpada u Koromačnom
content:
Burna rasprava
Skupština Istarske županije traži ukidanje odluke o spaljivanju otpada u Koromačnom
Županijska skupština Istarske županije izglasala je u ponedjeljak većinom glasova zaključak kojim od Vlade traži ukidanje odluke o spaljivanju otpada iz Gospića u cementari Holcim u Koromačnu, a protiv su bila četiri vijećnika HDZ-a.
Rasprava na tematskoj sjednici u Pazinu o odluci Vlade o zbrinjavanju dijela neopasnog otpada s lokacije PPK Velebit u tvornici cementa u Koromačnu potrajala je više sati, a zajednički zaključak poduprli su vijećnici s liste IDS-a, Nezavisne liste Borisa Miletića, SDP-a i Možemo!.
Donesena je i odluka o osnivanju radne skupina koja će kontrolirati kvalitetu zraka u okolici cementare Holcim u Koromačnu, na čijem će čelu bitipročelnik Upravnog odjela za održivi razvoj u županiji Mirko Radulović . Od Vlade traže da se svi podaci o nadzoru kvalitete zraka u Koromačnu na polusatnoj bazi automatski šalju Nastavnom zavodu za javno zdravstvo.
Istodobno, Skupština je pozdravila odluku Vlade da se riješi problem otpada u Pazinu i pozvala Vladu na poboljšanje dijaloga s lokalnom zajednicom i uključivanje stanovništva u sve takve odluke.
Istarski župan Boris Miletić kazao je kako je u cijelom slučaju izostala pravovremena i otvorena komunikacija s građanima i lokalnom samoupravom, dodavši kako je za odluku Vlade saznao iz medija.
"Vlada je donijela odluku o zbrinjavanju dijela otpada u dvije tvornice cementa, jednu u Koromačnu, drugu u Našicama, s pretpostavkom da se radi o neopasnom otpadu koji može biti uporabljen u fazi proizvodnje cementa u ove dvije tvornice, a za što tvornice posjeduju valjane okolišne i druge dozvole. Mislim da je to trebalo kvalitetnije i na vrijeme iskomunicirati i s načelnikom same općine i sa županijom", kazao je Miletić tijekom rasprave.
Istra i sama ima problema jer nema plan gospodarenja otpadom
Načelnik Općine Raša Leo Knapić rekao je da kao načelnik ima odgovornost prema ljudima koji žive u općini Raša i koji su s pravom zabrinuti za budućnost svog kraja, te je dužnost općine osigurati da se poštuju najviši ekološki standard.
SDP-ova Sanja Radolović rekla je da su prošle godine donesene izmjene i dopune Zakona o gospodarenju otpadom, upozorivši da Istarska županija nema plan gospodarenja otpadom nema. "Solidarni jesmo, ali Istra ima vlastite probleme u sustavu gospodarenja otpadom koje još uvijek nismo riješili", kazala je.
HDZ-ov vijećnik i načelnik Općine Sveti Petar u Šumi Mario Bratulić istaknuo da istarski HDZ ne traži bjanko obustavu dovoza otpada, ali ni ne umanjuje zabrinutost građana za cijeli slučaj.
"Tražimo pojačani nadzor svega što dolazi u Koromačno, ali i na Kaštijun. Mi smatramo da Holcim smije prihvatiti samo onu frakciju koja zadovoljava svu zakonsku proceduru i sve zakone. Predstavnici Holcima uložili su 37 milijuna eura kako bi mogli prihvaćati otpad s Kaštijuna i od velikih turističkih tvrtki", poručio je Bratulić.
Vijećnica Suzana Jašić (MOŽEMO!) poručila je kako građani Gospića kao ni građani Pazina nisu stvorili problem s otpadom, te da Labinština nije dužna prihvaćati gotove odluke, već je na državi da te probleme rješava na vrijeme i u suradnji s lokalnim zajednicama.
Direktor Fonda za zaštitu okoliša Luka Balen kazao kako razumije zabrinutost građana i javnosti u Gospiću Istri i u Našicama. Napravljene su dvije analize otpada, zaključeno je da se radi o 650 tona otpada u velikim vrećama, koje se nalaze u silosu, te su okarakterizirane kao neopasan otpad.
"To je mješavina otpadne plastike i frakcija višekratnih naslaga od mehaničke obrade, koji su okarakterizirani kao neopasan otpad", kazao je dodavši da 300 tona otpada ide u Holcim a 300 tona u Nexe, što to predstavlja ispod jedan posto kapaciteta godišnjeg otpada koji ta cementara obrađuje.
Cijeli proces zbrinjavanja neopasnog otpada iz Gospića će biti kontroliran i nama je cilj da se otpad zbrine, i sanira trajno, na zakonit način, kako bi se te lokacije vratile u prvobitne položaje, poručio je Balen.
Dodao je kako u Istri nije samo aktualna situacija oko otpada u Koromačnom, već i Pazinu gdje je, po prvim procjenama, gotovo 13.000 tona recikliranog otpadnog plastike, gume, tekstilnog otpada.
Kazao je i da je Vlada za Istarsku županiju osigurala gotovo 60-ak milijuna eura, od sredstava za izgradnju Kaštijuna i pretovarne stanice, kao i za odvojeno prikupljanje otpada i gotovo 4500 spremnika.

title: After Gujarat win, an emissions trading experiment heads to Rio
content:
In 2019, textile factory Swastik Poly Prints joined the emissions trading scheme (ETS) of Surat, a city in the Indian state of Gujarat. Since then, the company has reduced its particulate matter emissions by at least 30 per cent, claims its owner Binay Agrawal.
The ETS is a cap-and-trade system which seeks to curb air pollution by allowing companies to buy and sell permits for particulate matter emissions. Participating companies have access to an online dashboard which helps them track emissions. In Surat, factories like Swastik Poly Prints emitted 20-30 per cent less particulate pollution than those operating under conventional regulations, notes Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA), which brought the cap-and-trade system to Gujarat.
Agrawal says continuous emissions data via the ETS helped inform the company’s decisions on how to improve combustion efficiency, such as fine-tuning and upgrading its auto-firing systems, pollution-control equipment and filtration devices. Now, the company is “well within the limit” of its ETS cap, he notes.
Gujarat’s emissions trading scheme was a finalist for the 2025 Earthshot Prize hosted in Rio de Janeiro, where it piqued the interest of local officials. Now, the Brazilian city is exploring whether a similar market-based approach could help it tackle industrial pollution.
If implemented, this market would be the first of its kind in South America. A memorandum of understanding between EMA and the city of Rio, which would lay the foundations for the partnership, is now in legal review, says Kaushik Deb, executive director of EPIC India.
In June 2026, Rio de Janeiro announced a partnership with EMA. The accelerator is a partnership between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, a global research centre.
“
The aim is to reduce the total volume of emissions and enable this reduction to take place more efficiently – at a lower cost and in a manner better suited to each business’s specific profile.
Osmar Lima, secretary for economic development, Rio
According to Osmar Lima, Rio’s secretary for economic development, “some variables” are currently under assessment until June. These include “the pollutants that may be regulated, the facilities potentially covered, the emissions cap, the initial number of permits, the governance model, the trading platform and the monitoring, reporting and verification mechanisms”, Lima says.
Dialogue Earth spoke to researchers involved in the Gujarat experiment, the technical team working with Rio de Janeiro, and independent experts to examine what the model can deliver.
Gujarat’s results offer a promising proof of concept, with some high polluters showing lowered emissions. But questions remain over the transparency of emissions data, the capacity of regulators to run such markets and whether reductions in factory-level emissions translate into cleaner air for nearby communities, experts say.
Answers to those questions are important for Rio, which is still assessing whether a pollution-control model developed in an industrial hub in western India can work in its unique regulatory, industrial and environmental context.
“The idea at the outset is not just to set up an emissions trading scheme. We want to try and understand what the situation in Rio is,” Deb tells Dialogue Earth. Some lessons from Gujarat, including how to set an emissions cap and measure the total industrial emissions, may be transferable. But regulation, local laws and institutional capacity could prove harder to replicate, he notes.
The Surat model
Emissions trading is not a new concept. Over the years, markets for pollution control have cropped up in the United States and across Europe to reduce pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and greenhouse gases.
But Surat’s was the world’s first emissions trading scheme specifically targeting particulate matter, and in a polluted textile manufacturing hub.
The pilot in Surat covered 342 industrial units over seven months. A randomised selection of 168 participated in the scheme while 174 remained under conventional regulation. Participating plants reduced their particulate matter emissions by about 24 per cent compared with the control group. The latter failed to comply with pollution rules roughly a third of the time, while non-compliance fell to about 1 per cent among participants.
The market does not, however, replace regulation. It is a compliance market: regulators determine which industries participate, which pollutants are covered and how the cap is set. “Let’s say, in Gujarat, the initial cap was 280 [tonnes of particulate emission] and was reduced to 170 [tonnes] over two years,” says Dheeraj Alshetty, deputy director of EPIC India. The idea was to tighten the ceiling gradually rather than impose an immediate reduction that could result in major costs and resistance from industry, he adds.
At Swastik Poly Prints, the financial gain from selling surplus permits was one factor behind investment in cleaner technology, says Agrawal. But the bigger benefit was improved fuel efficiency. Better combustion reduced fuel consumption and costs, while also keeping the company comfortably within its emissions limit, he notes.
The hope is that these financial and reputational incentives encourage companies to invest in cleaner technology and more efficient production, Alshetty says.
Before the ETS was set up in parts of Gujarat, like other Indian states it relied on traditional “command-and-control” regulation. Under that system, regulators set emissions standards for industrial plants. “Compliance was expected and only non-compliance was penalised,” says Tejas Patel, deputy environmental engineer at the Gujarat Pollution Control Board. Plants that performed better had little financial incentive to reduce emissions further.
Under the ETS, the Gujarat Pollution Control Board set a ceiling for the combined emissions of participating industries, with companies receiving permits for a certain amount of pollution. Those that emit less than their allocation can sell surplus permits to companies that need additional allowances.
There are limits, however, on how much a company can rely on the market. In Gujarat, a firm can buy no more than 50 per cent above its initial allocation. Beyond that, the economics are designed to push firms towards cleaner technology or fuel, Alshetty notes.
Rio’s needs
After a year of preliminary talks, the EMA is currently working with Rio’s Department of Economic Development to hash out the details of this partnership, including establishing a roadmap and determining pollutants to focus on.
The City Council already has a voluntary tax incentive programme for companies that buy carbon credits. The city now wants to establish a new market for permits relating to particulate matter. This is where the EMA comes in.
“The aim is to reduce the total volume of emissions and enable this reduction to take place more efficiently – at a lower cost and in a manner better suited to each business’s specific profile,” says Lima.
But Rio’s pollution sources are different from Surat’s. Petrochemical and metalworking industries, as well as transport, are among the main drivers of pollution in Rio and nearby cities.
The city also has one of the highest levels of air pollution among Brazilian state capitals and is second only to São Paulo in pollution-related deaths, recording around 17,000 between 2023 and 2025, according to estimates from the Ministry of Health.
“It is necessary to consider where emissions are concentrated, who is exposed to them, and whether the regulatory framework prevents the formation or persistence of pollution hotspots,” notes Carolina Mendes Rocha, a carbon specialist at the E+ Institute, a Brazilian think-tank focused on the energy transition. “A system may fully meet its aggregate reduction target and yet still allow excessive concentrations of pollutants in certain neighbourhoods or communities,” she says.
Cleaner air?
The results of the Gujarat experiment are promising, but they come with important limitations. The pilot measured emissions from industrial stacks, not ambient PM10 or PM2.5, which is the pollution people inhale and includes sources like heavy vehicles and construction activity.
The Surat experiment also focused on textiles, an industry where pollution controls are relatively limited, notes Bhargav Krishna, coordinator for environmental governance and policy at the Sustainable Futures Collaborative. “It’s debatable whether it would be equally effective for steel, cement, power industries, which have a more complex political economy around them.”
“An effective ETS should not focus only on particles but also gases such as SO2 [sulphur dioxide] and NO2 [nitrous dioxide],” says Krishna, noting that secondary particles can make up a substantial share of particulate pollution. SO2 emissions are mainly generated by burning fossil fuels.
An SO2 ETS is being designed in other Indian states drawing on Gujarat’s experience, according to Patel. This demonstrates that the model is not tied to a specific sector, he adds.
One example is Maharashtra, which is developing an SO2 market for several industries. It could offer lessons on technology adoption, costs and emissions reductions, notes Abinaya Sekar, an air quality scientist working with the Health Effects Institute.
Patel says a direct measurement of the ETS’s impact on ambient air quality has not yet been conducted. But he opines that stack-level emission reduction across hundreds of industrial units could translate into meaningful improvements in air quality in and around Surat.
The city’s experiment shows ETS is a viable mechanism for the Global South, he says. Alshetty estimates 80-85 per cent of the model can be transferred across states, with the rest customised based on local conditions such as fuel availability and industry composition.
Not so easy
It took the Gujarat government around nine years to launch the market. Continuous emissions monitoring systems (CEMS) were installed starting from 2014, with guidelines coming in 2018 and the market following in 2019, Alshetty says.
But the data generated by CEMS is still not publicly available, says Krishna, making it difficult for independent researchers and the public to assess emission levels and the market’s performance.
Krishna believes the model worked partly because three conditions came together: a highly capable technical institution in the form of the EMA and ETS, strong attention from the state government, and rapid deployment of technologies to monitor and control emissions. India’s state pollution-control boards “certainly do not possess the capabilities to do so” as they continue to face staffing and institutional capacity constraints, he says.
Krishna also cautions against replacing traditional models with market-based regulation. “The existing regulatory system is broken, no doubt, but the answer to me isn’t to chuck it out in favour of a market-based mechanism,” he says. Rather, the system should be strengthened and equipped to handle current and future challenges.
“The Surat experiment gives us a strong counterfactual between the emissions trading market and the status-quo regulatory system,” says Sekar. But to draw a fair comparison between the two, researchers would need to compare the market with an equally resourced conventional approach, she says.

title: Bhat-Bhateni rebuilds 10 stores damaged during Gen Z uprising
content:
Money
Bhat-Bhateni rebuilds 10 stores damaged during Gen Z uprising
Despite the destruction and damage to its stores on September 9, 2025, the supermarket chain continued paying over 10,000 employees and began clearing debris within a week.Yagya Banjade
A year ago, Bhat-Bhateni Supermarket, Nepal’s largest retail chain, faced one of the biggest crises in its four-decades-long history.
On the second day of the Gen Z uprising on September 9, 2025, twelve of its outlets and its Baluwatar warehouse were completely destroyed or gutted while several others outlets were vandalised and looted.
The company has since rebuilt and reopened 10 of the 12 severely damaged outlets, with its Damak and Hetauda stores expected to resume operations by December and January, respectively.
“There was pain in our hearts and tears in our eyes as we watched our stores burn,” said Chairman and Managing Director Min Bahadur Gurung on Monday while reopening Bhat-Bhateni’s outlet in Tangal. “But we didn’t forget our responsibility towards the state and our employees. We started work within a week, clearing hot ash, steel rods and bricks, and have managed to reopen 10 stores in a year.”
The recovery stands out against the scale of the damage. The company reported losses of more than Rs11 billion after the protests. Bhat-Bhateni filed a claim exceeding Rs11 billion across 20 stores, including 12 that were completely destroyed. More than Rs500 million worth of goods were reportedly looted.
The Post reported that 21 of Bhat-Bhateni’s 28 outlets were damaged during the unrest. The attacks came on September 9, a day after dozens of protesters were shot dead during anti-corruption demonstrations that were triggered by social media ban. Bhat-Bhateni was among the private businesses targeted by protesters amid anger towards political parties and figures associated with the then ruling CPN-UML. Gurung had drawn controversy in 2024 after donating land for the UML’s central office.
For Bhat-Bhateni, the destruction also threatened thousands of jobs. Around 5,000 of its roughly 10,000 employees worked at the affected outlets and warehouse.
“Although our business infrastructure was destroyed, the company decided not to remove employees from their jobs,” said chief operation officer Panu Paudel. “We retained more than 10,000 employees and also paid the festival [Dashain] bonus that was due after the Gen Z movement.
Rebuilding began within days and continued around the clock. Teams had to reconstruct buildings, electrical and technical systems, equipment, sales areas, storage arrangements and customer service facilities.
“This was not an ordinary reconstruction,” said Paudel. “We had to rebuild the entire system needed to operate a store. We worked 24 hours a day. Once one store was ready, teams moved to the next.”
The Baluwatar warehouse, crucial to the company’s supply chain, was brought back into operation within 70 days. The Koteshwar outlet followed within four months. Maharajgunj, Chitwan, Pokhara, Baudha, Biratnagar, Birtamod, and Dharan have since reopened, with Tangal, the chain’s first-ever outlet, becoming the latest to resume operations.
The company estimates that rebuilding the 12 severely damaged outlets will cost about Rs15 billion. Paudel said work on the remaining two is progressing, with Damak targeted for reopening in December and Hetauda in January.
The recovery comes as businesses across the country continue to deal with the wider economic fallout of the September unrest.
Before the unrest, the affected outlets were among Bhat-Bhateni’s major revenue-generating stores. The company reported average daily transactions of about Rs105 million across its network. Reopening them therefore meant restoring not just buildings, but the supply chain and customer-service systems supporting thousands of jobs.
For Gurung, rebuilding quickly was also about keeping the company functioning and its employees at work. “We considered our work a duty to the country and its citizens,” he said. “We moved forward despite everything that had happened.”

title: Somalia-Pakistan deepen technical cooperation on digital transformation
content:
Friday September 18, 2026
The mission was jointly organized by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) country offices in Pakistan and Somalia. During the visit, Somali officials held meetings with Pakistani institutions involved in digital identity, digital government, social protection, taxation, digital payments and citizen services.
A high-level Somali delegation has concluded a 10-day peer learning mission to Pakistan aimed at exploring ways to strengthen Somalia’s digital public ecosystem and improve digital public services.
The delegation was led by Abdiwali Ali Abdulle, Director General of Somalia’s National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA), and included senior representatives from NIRA, the Ministry of Finance, the Central Bank of Somalia and other financial and development institutions.
The delegation visited the National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) to learn about Pakistan’s national identity system and its institutional framework. It also held discussions with the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication and other digital institutions on digital public infrastructure, interoperability and the development of a national data exchange layer.
In Lahore, the delegation visited an e-Khidmat Centre to observe how multiple government services are provided to citizens through an integrated digital platform.
Officials also visited the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP), where they reviewed Pakistan’s National Socio-Economic Registry and digital social protection payment mechanisms. Discussions with the Federal Board of Revenue focused on the use of digital identity and data integration for taxpayer registration.
The State Bank of Pakistan briefed the delegation on Raast, Pakistan’s instant payment system, as well as the banking sector’s shared electronic know-your-customer (e-KYC) platform. A session with civil society organizations also focused on reaching women, displaced populations and communities facing barriers to registration.Finance
The mission concluded with the Somalia-Pakistan Technical Cooperation Roundtable, attended by Senate Chairman Syed Yousaf Raza Gilani as the chief guest. The meeting brought together senior representatives of participating institutions to discuss lessons learned, partnership priorities and future areas of technical cooperation.
“Digital governance is an important instrument for improving public service delivery, institutional efficiency, accountability and citizen inclusion,” Gilani said. He added that parliament had an important role in ensuring that digital transformation remained inclusive, secure, accountable and rights-based, highlighting the Senate of Pakistan’s move towards a paperless e-Parliament.
Abdiwali Ali Abdulle said the mission provided Somalia with an opportunity to learn from Pakistan’s experience and identify practices that could be adapted to the Somali context.
He said Pakistan had valuable experience in digital identity, digital finance, social protection and interoperability, while Somalia’s experience with mobile money and rapid digital adoption could also provide lessons for Pakistan.
The participants also validated the Somalia-Pakistan Partnership Action Matrix, outlining areas for continued cooperation in foundational and legal identity, digital public infrastructure and governance, interoperability, secure data exchange, financial inclusion and digital public financing.
Jama Hassan, Counsellor at the Embassy of Somalia, said the programme provided valuable insight into Pakistan’s functional identity and wider e-governance systems.
“Functional identity is not synonymous with number or databases,” he said, highlighting the importance of linking identity systems with access to public services.
Dr. Samuel Rizk, Resident Representative of UNDP Pakistan, said legal identity was fundamental to inclusive governance and helped people access services, social protection and financial opportunities.
He said UNDP’s partnership with NADRA in Pakistan had helped more than one million women obtain identity documents, adding that the Somalia mission was focused on sharing these lessons while promoting trust, inclusion and data protection alongside technological development.

title: 「配偶者」の定義変えた法人 多様な性学ぶ研修、当事者は問いかけた
content:
「配偶者」とはなんだろう。
パートナーを亡くしたとき、介護を迫られたとき、住宅手当を申請するとき。家族を支えるための制度が、受けられないひとがいる。
札幌市の社会福祉法人「札幌恵友会」で7月末、施設長ら14人を対象に性的マイノリティーへの理解を深める研修があった。
法人は4月に、就業規則の配偶者を「異性であるか同性であるかを問わず、事実上婚姻関係と同様の事情にある者」と大きく広げた。職員らでつくる「札幌地域労働組合恵友会支部」の組合員たちが提案し、認められた。研修も職員からの働きかけだ。
講師を務めたのは女装家、満島てる子さん（36）。多様な性が自然に受け入れられる社会にしたいと活動している。
会場に問いかけた。
「LGBTQ、少し前まで『性的少数者』と書かれていることが多かったと思います。少なそうですよね。何人に1人ぐらいでしょうか？」
100人、50人、25人、10人……。それぞれパラパラと手が上がる。
「正解は約10人に1人です。決して少ないとは言えないんですよね」
満島さんは日本人に多いとされる名字を読み上げる。「佐藤さん、鈴木さん、高橋さん、田中さん、まとめて人口の5%。LGBTQの方がパーセンテージ多いんです」
そして続けた。「当事者に出会ったことがない、という人がいるかもしれない。それは相当数の当事者が、当事者であることを公言していないことに由来します」
企業が変わり始めている。これまで「男女」の枠で作っていた制度を変更する会社が増えた。一方、制度を変えたからといって、全員の理解が一気に進むわけではない。
満島さんは、就業規則の変化を評価する一方、「制度が変わったことの意味を、職場の中でしっかりと伝えてください」と念を押す。その上で、LGBTQが職場で直面しがちな問題を自身の経験を交えながら話した。
